title: Floquet Abelian Multicycle Codes
abstract: Abelian multicycle (AMC) codes are compact quantum low-density parity-check codes whose multiblock chain-complex structure provides redundant low-weight stabilizers and supports single-shot error correction. We introduce Floquet AMC codes by deriving a quotient-lattice representation of a general level-$j$, $D$-dimensional AMC complex over a finite Abelian group algebra, lifting this lattice to spacetime, and rotating the circuit-time direction in the associated ZX network. When the check and data spiders have even valence and admit a time-oriented local port matching, the network decomposes into a periodic schedule of native two-qubit $XX$ and $ZZ$ measurements. We construct generalized-bicycle and level-$2$ AMC4 examples, determine their instantaneous stabilizer groups, and compute their embedded distances by minimizing over all inequivalent circuit cuts. For AMC4 instances locally equivalent to four-dimensional toric codes, we obtain Floquet memories with parameters $[[108,6,5]]$, $[[144,6,8]]$, and $[[324,6,10]]$. Local Pauli-web detector templates and beam-search decoding under the measurement-native EM3 noise model yield an estimated pseudothreshold of approximately $1.2\%$. These results provide compact measurement-only realizations of higher-dimensional homological redundancy without directly measuring the original weight-six stabilizers.
summary: The paper introduces Floquet Abelian Multicycle (AMC) codes, extending compact qLDPC codes to incorporate higher-dimensional homological redundancy. By mapping these structures onto a periodic measurement schedule using ZX networks, they achieve error correction through native two-qubit Pauli measurements. This results in concrete quantum memories with improved performance metrics compared to standard constructions.
main_problem: The goal is to develop compact quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes that can realize higher-dimensional homological redundancy while supporting single-shot error correction via measurement-only protocols.
main_result: The authors constructed Floquet Abelian Multicycle (AMC) codes, yielding specific examples like [[144, 6, 8]] with an estimated pseudothreshold of approximately 1.2% under EM3 noise.
method: They derive these codes by lifting the quotient-lattice representation of a general AMC complex to spacetime and rotating the circuit time direction in an associated ZX network.
model_or_system: The system is based on Abelian multicycle (AMC) codes, which are defined using chain complexes over finite Abelian group algebras. The resulting structure is realized as a periodic measurement schedule involving native two-qubit XX and ZZ measurements.
key_observables: Embedded distances ($	ext{d}_{	ext{emb}}$), logical error rates vs. physical noise rate ($p$), and the Bravyi–Poulin–Terhal (BPT) metric.
important_parameters: Code parameters such as $[[108, 6, 5]]$, $[[144, 6, 8]]$, and $[[324, 6, 10]]$ for AMC4 instances; the noise model is EM3.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that when check and data spiders have even valence, the network decomposes into native two-qubit Pauli measurements. Distance calculations rely on Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the decomposition of complex measurement structures ('spiders') into pairwise measurements using a 'Stairway' construction, and plot logical failure probability versus physical noise rate for specific codes.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework by defining AMC codes via group algebras. It then introduces Floquetization by lifting this structure to spacetime and decomposing it into periodic two-qubit measurements. Finally, concrete examples are constructed, their distances calculated, and performance is evaluated under noise models.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly structured, measurement-based approach to quantum error correction that moves beyond simple planar geometries (like surface codes) by encoding redundancy in the spacetime structure of the stabilizer measurements.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Spiders as check measurements for the case with no output states. Here b is an integer that describes the measurement parity. The number of qubits is arbitrary and depends on the particular stabilizer code. The color indicates whether the measured parity is Z-type or X- type.

FIG. 2. Unrotated check-measurement network. Data- qubit worldlines run vertically through alternating check- measurement layers. The unrotated network can be viewed as a syndrome-extraction circuit drawn in ZX notation.
FIG. 3. Stairway-style decomposition of many-leg spiders into pairwise measurements. The measured Pauli type is inherited from the spider color, pink (X) or green (Z).

FIG. 4. Intracell edges and external connection bundles for the AMC4 half-cells over an arbitrary finite Abelian group algebra. The thin colored lines inside each dashed box are the identity-term intracell incidences. Each thick J-colored stub represents the nonidentity support terms of aJ: a bundle containing j ∈JJ, with |JJ| = wt(aJ) −1. For each j ∈JGX(J,p), one strand connects XJ(u) to qp(u −j), whereas on the data side it connects qp(u) to XJ(u + j). For the strand bundle JGZ(J,p) the signs are reversed. Arrowheads indicate the relative displacement toward the neighboring cell, not an orientation of the Tanner edge.

FIG. 5. Local incidence diagram for a GB code with weight-four checks. A unit cell containing two qubits and two checks is split into two half-unit cells of X- and Z-type. Each half-unit cell has nin = 4 inputs. Within each half-unit cell, each data node is turned into a spider by adding extra τin and τout ports. Local objects are labeled with superscript (0), while external ports are labeled by relative lattice directions such as q−jA and X+jB. The colors mark the chosen port matching for the corresponding check–data ZX network. In addition, X spiders are marked by pink and Z spiders are marked by green.
